q: Find \( x \) and \( y \) in this matrix equation \( \begin{pmatrix} x+y \\ x-y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \begin{pmatrix} x+y \\ x-y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} \)


\( x + y = 8 \quad \cdots\ (1) \)


\( x - y = 2 \quad \cdots\ (2) \)


Step 2

Adding (1) and (2), we get \( 2x = 10 \).

Step 3

So \( x = 5 \) and hence, from (1), \( y = 3 \).

Final Answer:

\( x = 5,\ y = 3 \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 7 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( A + B \) and \( B + A \). What law does this illustrate?
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( A + B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 7 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1+0 & 2+2 \\ 4+7 & 5+3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 11 & 8 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( B + A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 7 & 3 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 11 & 8 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

Thus \( A + B = B + A \). Matrix addition is commutative.

Final Answer:

\( A + B = B + A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 11 & 8 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Given that \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( 3A - 2B \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( 3A = 3\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 12 & 9 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( 2B = 2\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 10 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( 3A - 2B = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 12 & 9 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 10 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -7 \\ 12 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -7 \\ 12 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Solve \( 3\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} - 2X = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \) for the \( 2 \times 2 \) matrix \( X \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( 3\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} - 2X = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)


\( \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} - 2X = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

Add the negative of \( \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \) to both sides.

\( O - 2X = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \)


\( -2X = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

Multiply by \( -\dfrac{1}{2} \).

\( X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Given \( X = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( Y = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( XY \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( XY = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( = \begin{pmatrix} (2\times 1)+(1\times 3) & (2\times 2)+(1\times 1) & (2\times 3)+(1\times 0) \\ (4\times 1)+(0\times 3) & (4\times 2)+(0\times 1) & (4\times 3)+(0\times 0) \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 & 6 \\ 4 & 8 & 12 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 & 6 \\ 4 & 8 & 12 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Given \( P = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( PQ \) and \( QP \). What do you notice?
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( PQ = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2+2 & 8+1 \\ 0+6 & 0+3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 9 \\ 6 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( QP = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2+0 & 1+12 \\ 4+0 & 2+3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 13 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

Notice that \( PQ \ne QP \), so multiplication of matrices is not commutative.

Final Answer:

\( PQ = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 9 \\ 6 & 3 \end{pmatrix},\ QP = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 13 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix},\ PQ \ne QP \)

q: If \( A = (4\\ 1) \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \), which of the products \( AB \), \( BA \) are possible? Simplify those products that exist.
c:
Solution:

Step 1

Order of \( A \) is \( 1 \times 2 \) and order of \( B \) is \( 2 \times 2 \). The inner numbers are the same, so \( AB \) exists and has order \( 1 \times 2 \).

Step 2

\( AB = (4\ 1)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = (4+3,\ 8-1) = (7\ 7) \)


Step 3

Order of \( B \) is \( 2 \times 2 \) and order of \( A \) is \( 1 \times 2 \). The inner numbers 2 and 1 are different, so \( BA \) does not exist.

Final Answer:

\( AB = (7\ 7) \); \( BA \) does not exist.

q: Given \( \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} \), find a system of equations in \( x \) and \( y \). Hence find \( x \) and \( y \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} \)


\( \begin{pmatrix} 4x+y \\ 3x-y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} \)


The system is \( 4x + y = 9 \), \( 3x - y = 5 \).

Step 2

Adding these two equations, we get \( 7x = 14 \), so \( x = 2 \).

Step 3

Substituting \( x = 2 \) into \( 4x + y = 9 \) gives \( 8 + y = 9 \), so \( y = 1 \).

Final Answer:

\( x = 2,\ y = 1 \)

q: Find the products \( \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \). What do you notice?
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8+0 & 0+3 \\ 5+0 & 0+2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8+0 & 3+0 \\ 0+5 & 0+2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

So \( AI = IA = A \). The unit matrix behaves like 1 in ordinary arithmetic.

Final Answer:

\( AI = IA = A \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( AB \) and \( BA \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( AB = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4-4 & 4-4 \\ -2+2 & -2+2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = O \)


Step 2

\( BA = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4-2 & -8+4 \\ 2-1 & -4+2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

Note that \( AB = O \) does not mean that \( A = O \) or \( B = O \).

Final Answer:

\( AB = O,\ BA = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( p \) and \( q \) such that \( A^2 = pA + qI \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ 5 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( pA + qI = p\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} + q\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2p+q & p \\ p & 3p+q \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

Hence \( p = 5 \) and \( 2p + q = 5 \), so \( q = -5 \).

Final Answer:

\( p = 5,\ q = -5 \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \), show that \( A \) and \( B \) are inverses of each other.
c:
Solution:

Step 1

We have to show that \( AB = I = BA \).

Step 2

\( AB = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9-8 & -6+6 \\ 12-12 & -8+9 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I \)


Step 3

\( BA = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9-8 & 6-6 \\ -12+12 & -8+9 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I \)


Since \( AB = I = BA \), \( A \) and \( B \) are inverses of each other.

Final Answer:

\( AB = BA = I \)

q: Find, if it exists, the inverse matrix of \( M = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \det M = (3)(2) - (5)(1) = 6 - 5 = 1 \ne 0 \)
, so \( M^{-1} \) exists.

Step 2

\( M^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det M}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

Thus \( M^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \).

Final Answer:

\( M^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Solve the matrix equation \( \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} X = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \) for the \( 2 \times 2 \) matrix \( X \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

Let \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \). Then \( \det A = (2)(1) - (1)(1) = 1 \).

Step 2

\( A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \)


\( AX = B \implies A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B \implies IX = A^{-1}B \implies X = A^{-1}B \)


Step 3

\( X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Let \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \). Find \( A^{-1} \) and hence the matrix \( P \) such that \( AP = B \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \det A = 3 - 2 = 1 \)
, so \( A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 2

From \( AP = B \), pre-multiply by \( A^{-1} \): \( A^{-1}AP = A^{-1}B \), so \( P = A^{-1}B \).

Step 3

\( P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2-0 & 1-1 \\ -4+0 & -2+3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( P = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Using the matrices of the previous type, if \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( Q \) such that \( QA = B \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

From \( QA = B \), post-multiply by \( A^{-1} \): \( QAA^{-1} = BA^{-1} \), so \( Q = BA^{-1} \).

Step 2

\( A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( Q = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2-2 & -2+3 \\ 0-2 & 0+3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( 2A + 3B \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( 2A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 6 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( 3B = \begin{pmatrix} -3 & 12 \\ 6 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( 2A + 3B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 6 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} -3 & 12 \\ 6 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 16 \\ 12 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 16 \\ 12 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( A^2 \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

By definition, \( A^2 = AA \).

Step 2

\( A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1+0 & 2+2 \\ 0+0 & 0+1 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: If \( A^T - \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 & 5 \\ 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix} \), find the \( 2 \times 2 \) matrix \( A \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( A^T = \begin{pmatrix} 9 & 5 \\ 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 12 & 6 \\ 4 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

The matrix whose transpose is \( A^T \) is obtained by writing rows of \( A^T \) as columns.

Step 3

\( A = \begin{pmatrix} 12 & 4 \\ 6 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( A = \begin{pmatrix} 12 & 4 \\ 6 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: A shopper buys 3 shirts, 1 blouse and 2 skirts. The prices in kyat at two shops are given by the rate matrix \( R = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 20 & 25 \\ 15 & 12 \end{pmatrix} \). If the quantities matrix is \( Q = (3\ 1\ 2) \), find \( QR \) and interpret the result.
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( Q \) is \( 1 \times 3 \) and \( R \) is \( 3 \times 2 \), so \( QR \) is \( 1 \times 2 \).

Step 2

\( QR = (3\ 1\ 2)\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 20 & 25 \\ 15 & 12 \end{pmatrix} = (3\times 10+1\times 20+2\times 15,\ 3\times 8+1\times 25+2\times 12) \)


Step 3

\( = (80\ 73) \)


The total cost is 80 kyats at the first shop and 73 kyats at the second shop.

Final Answer:

\( (80\ 73) \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 20 & 25 \\ 15 & 12 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( AB \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( A \) is \( 2 \times 3 \) and \( B \) is \( 3 \times 2 \), so \( AB \) is \( 2 \times 2 \).

Step 2

Row 1 of \( AB \) is \( (3\times 10+1\times 20+2\times 15,\ 3\times 8+1\times 25+2\times 12) = (80,\ 73) \).

Step 3

Row 2 of \( AB \) is \( (1\times 10+2\times 20+1\times 15,\ 1\times 8+2\times 25+1\times 12) = (65,\ 70) \).

\( AB = \begin{pmatrix} 80 & 73 \\ 65 & 70 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( \begin{pmatrix} 80 & 73 \\ 65 & 70 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Find \( x \) and \( y \) if \( \begin{pmatrix} x+2y \\ 3x-2y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( x + 2y = 11 \quad \cdots\ (1) \)


\( 3x - 2y = 1 \quad \cdots\ (2) \)


Step 2

Adding (1) and (2), we get \( 4x = 12 \), so \( x = 3 \).

Step 3

Substituting \( x = 3 \) into (1) gives \( 3 + 2y = 11 \), so \( y = 4 \).

Final Answer:

\( x = 3,\ y = 4 \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} k & 1 \\ 0 & k \end{pmatrix} \), find \( A^2 \) and \( A^3 \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( A^2 = AA = \begin{pmatrix} k & 1 \\ 0 & k \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} k & 1 \\ 0 & k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} k^2 & 2k \\ 0 & k^2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( A^3 = A^2 A = \begin{pmatrix} k^2 & 2k \\ 0 & k^2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} k & 1 \\ 0 & k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} k^3 & 3k^2 \\ 0 & k^3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

In general the pattern is \( A^n = \begin{pmatrix} k^n & n k^{n-1} \\ 0 & k^n \end{pmatrix} \).

Final Answer:

\( A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} k^2 & 2k \\ 0 & k^2 \end{pmatrix},\ A^3 = \begin{pmatrix} k^3 & 3k^2 \\ 0 & k^3 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Find the two matrices of the form \( X = \begin{pmatrix} x & 1 \\ 0 & y \end{pmatrix} \) such that \( X^2 = I \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( X^2 = \begin{pmatrix} x & 1 \\ 0 & y \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x & 1 \\ 0 & y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x^2 & x+y \\ 0 & y^2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( \begin{pmatrix} x^2 & x+y \\ 0 & y^2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)


\( x^2 = 1 \), \( x + y = 0 \), \( y^2 = 1 \).

Step 3

So \( x = \pm 1 \) and \( y = -x \). The two matrices are \( \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \).

Final Answer:

\( \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{and}\ \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Solve \( 2X - \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 & 5 \\ 2 & 8 \end{pmatrix} \) for \( X \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( 2X = \begin{pmatrix} 9 & 5 \\ 2 & 8 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 12 & 6 \\ 6 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

Multiply by \( \dfrac{1}{2} \).

Step 3

\( X = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( X = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \)

q: Verify that \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \) satisfies \( A^2 - 2A + I = O \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9-4 & -12+4 \\ 3-1 & -4+1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & -8 \\ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( 2A = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & -8 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( A^2 - 2A + I = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & -8 \\ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 6 & -8 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = O \)


Final Answer:

\( A^2 - 2A + I = O \)

q: Given that \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \), \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & a \\ c & 4 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( C = \begin{pmatrix} b & 6 \\ 4 & d \end{pmatrix} \), find \( a, b, c \) and \( d \) if \( 2A + B = C \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( 2A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( 2A + B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 5 & a \\ c & 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 & a-4 \\ c+4 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

This equals \( C = \begin{pmatrix} b & 6 \\ 4 & d \end{pmatrix} \), so \( b = 9 \), \( a - 4 = 6 \), \( c + 4 = 4 \), \( d = 10 \). Hence \( a = 10 \), \( b = 9 \), \( c = 0 \), \( d = 10 \).

Final Answer:

\( a = 10,\ b = 9,\ c = 0,\ d = 10 \)

q: Find the values of \( a \) and \( b \) if \( \begin{pmatrix} a & 2a \\ 2b & b \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 33 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix} \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \begin{pmatrix} 3a+8a \\ 6b+4b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 33 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 2

\( \begin{pmatrix} 11a \\ 10b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 33 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( 11a = 33 \implies a = 3 \)
and
\( 10b = 50 \implies b = 5 \)


Final Answer:

\( a = 3,\ b = 5 \)

q: If \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( A^{-1} \) and verify that \( A A^{-1} = I \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \det A = 6 - 5 = 1 \)
, so \( A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 2

\( A A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6-5 & -2+2 \\ 15-15 & -5+6 \end{pmatrix} \)


Step 3

\( = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I \)


Final Answer:

\( A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{pmatrix},\ A A^{-1} = I \)

q: Given \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \), \( B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \) and \( C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \), find \( X \) if \( AX = C \).
c:
Solution:

Step 1

\( \det A = 2 - 0 = 2 \)
, so \( A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 2

From \( AX = C \), \( X = A^{-1}C \).

Step 3

\( X = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \)


Final Answer:

\( X = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \)
